dearth

/durth/ — rhymes with birth · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A dearth is a scarcity or lack of something that is needed or expected to be there.

The coach complained about a dearth of tall players on this year's roster.

Example

The desert town faced a dearth of clean water, forcing residents to drive forty miles for supplies.

Dearth emphasizes not just lack, but a serious shortage of something essential and expected. It is more precise than the plain word 'shortage' because it conveys the gravity and critical nature of the situation.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

shortfall: A shortfall is the measurable gap between what you have and what you need — the budget came up ten thousand dollars short. It is neutral and numerical. A dearth is weightier: a serious, formal word for the troubling scarcity of something people expected to be there.

insufficiency: Insufficiency measures an amount against a purpose: there is some, but too little to be enough for the job. A dearth is a heavier, more literary word — it says something needed is strikingly scarce, and it carries a gravity that plain insufficiency does not.

paucity: Paucity means a very small, meager supply, and like dearth it is a formal word. The difference is emphasis: paucity points at how tiny the amount is, while a dearth stresses that something needed or expected is missing — a felt absence, not just a small count.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

abundance: a large supply, more than enough

surplus: an extra amount beyond what is needed

Where it sits · how severe the scarcity is — lack → shortage → dearth → famine

lack vs. dearth: A lack is milder than a dearth: a lack just means something is missing, while a dearth is a serious, noticeable scarcity of something people count on.

shortage vs. dearth: A shortage is weaker than a dearth — a shortage is often temporary and fixable, while a dearth suggests a striking, troubling scarcity of something expected to be there.

famine vs. dearth: A famine is far stronger than a dearth: a dearth of food means food is scarce, but a famine means so little food exists that people starve.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — dear (Old English dēore)

Root — dear (Old English dēore): precious, costly (Old English)

Suffix — -th

Suffix — -th: state or condition of (forms nouns, as in warmth, growth) (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Dear once meant 'costly,' and -th turns an adjective into a noun naming a state — so dearth literally meant 'costliness.' When something is scarce it becomes costly, which is exactly how dearth came to mean a scarcity of something needed or expected.

Use the root in a new word: endearing

Use the root in a new word: endearing: The puppy's endearing head-tilt made everyone hold it dear — 'precious' — the same root dear that hides at the start of dearth.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Dearth is formal and literary—reach for it when you need gravity, when discussing something critically needed that is missing. For everyday shortage or insufficient supply, simpler words like 'lack' or 'shortage' are better choices.
